Singapore billionaire Forrest Li's Sea plans new cloud business, IPO for financial services arm --> China asks citizens to watch out for scams, kidnappings in Thailand By Thao Anh October 20, 2026 | 12:38 am PT Get VnExpress first in Google Search See more of the news you trust. Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results The Chinese embassy in Thailand has issued an urgent safety advisory for its citizens traveling to or residing in the country following a rising incidence of forced labor, human trafficking, and bogus job offers. According to an embassy notice published on Oct. 16, travelers are advised to carefully plan their itineraries, pay strict attention to transport security, and remain highly vigilant against fraudulent schemes.
It has been widely reported that transnational criminal networks operate multibillion-dollar scam compounds along the Thailand–Myanmar border, using lucrative job advertisements to lure victims into forced labor and online fraud operations.
Criminal groups are increasingly targeting individuals in livestreaming, performance arts, and creative industries by issuing fake audition invites, filming project contracts, or business exchange proposals as a cover for human trafficking.
Tourists in Bangkok's Chinatown, Thailand, Jan. 19, 2023. Photo by Reuters
Prominent cases covered by the media illustrate the severity of the crisis.
In one major case detailed by SCMP , actor Wang Xing was lured to Thailand in January 2025 under the guise of a fake filming project before being abducted to a scam compound in Myanmar.
According to a documentary by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV , Wang was resold across three different scam operations within just four days before Chinese embassy officials successfully negotiated his release.
Though he returned to China safely, he remains burdened by massive online loans he was forced to take out while captive.
Other recent disappearances have further alarmed the public.
In August, The Nation reported that a Chinese tourist was abducted in Thailand after getting into a vehicle she mistook for that of her tour guide, freeing herself only after shouting for help at a police checkpoint.
Citing an urgent social media post on Oct. 1, China Daily wrote about the disappearance of a music teacher from Shanghai who went missing in Thailand on Sept. 25.
Global Times reported that, on Oct. 5, a 34-year-old Chinese photographer went missing after traveling to Bangkok for a shooting assignment, prompting his family to report an abduction following a ransom demand.
In light of these incidents, diplomatic officials detailed safety instructions for travelers.
Chinese citizens are urged to verify all overseas job offers and investment projects.
They should be wary of social media posts or personal recommendations that promise high salaries, vague job roles, easy hiring criteria, or free trips without requiring prior experience.
Travelers should plan ahead, use legitimate transport services, refuse rides from strangers, and decline unexpected changes to routes or meeting spots.
Besides, travel to high-risk border regions near Myanmar should be avoided.
Officials advise travelers to keep family members informed of their whereabouts, maintain phone accessibility, and never hand over passports or bank cards to third parties.
